title: The Pit and the Pendulum

teacherSummary.text: Condemned by the Spanish Inquisition in Toledo, the narrator wakes in a pitch-dark cell. He narrowly avoids falling into a central pit, then wakes strapped beneath a razor-edged pendulum descending toward his heart. He smears food on his bonds so rats chew them free. The walls then glow red-hot and close in, forcing him toward the pit, until a French army takes Toledo and General Lasalle catches his arm.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this story is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “The Pit and the Pendulum,” how does Poe show reason struggling against terror? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the imagery you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In The Pit and the Pendulum, how does Poe develop the idea of reason struggling against terror? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the imagery in the story helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how The Pit and the Pendulum develops the idea of reason struggling against terror. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of imagery and structure shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of The Pit and the Pendulum (where it begins, turns and ends) and its imagery shape the reader's understanding of reason struggling against terror. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what The Pit and the Pendulum suggests about reason struggling against terror. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the story's imagery and structure), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Edgar Allan Poe uses imagery in The Pit and the Pendulum to complicate the reader's understanding of reason struggling against terror. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate The Pit and the Pendulum within its historical and literary context and argue how the story's treatment of reason struggling against terror responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read The Pit and the Pendulum alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the story's handling of reason struggling against terror follows or bends those conventions, using the imagery as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to The Pit and the Pendulum and its treatment of reason struggling against terror. State your method, show what it reveals in the story's imagery and structure, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads The Pit and the Pendulum as evidence for a larger claim about reason struggling against terror in The Pit and the Pendulum. Connect close reading of the story to the whole story, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads The Pit and the Pendulum as a hinge in the story's larger treatment of reason struggling against terror. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on The Pit and the Pendulum.

satQuestions.passage: Very suddenly there came back to my soul motion and sound—the tumultuous motion of the heart, and, in my ears, the sound of its beating. Then a pause in which all is blank. Then again sound, and motion, and touch—a tingling sensation pervading my frame. Then the mere consciousness of existence, without thought—a condition which lasted long. Then, very suddenly, thought, and shuddering terror, and earnest endeavor to comprehend my true state. Then a strong desire to lapse into insensibility. Then a rushing revival of soul and a successful effort to move. And now a full memory of the trial, of the judges, of the sable draperies, of the sentence, of the sickness, of the swoon. Then entire forgetfulness of all that followed; of all that a later day and much earnestness of endeavor have enabled me vaguely to recall.

segments.script: Annotate the story for pacing, imagery (three marks with a margin note each), then write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph: what does this story suggest about reason struggling against terror? Then start your writing prompt at your assigned level (HS Sophomore: Analyze how The Pit and the Pendulum develops the idea of reason struggling against terror. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of imagery and structure shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) Exemplar: Poe builds suspense by slowing time to the speed of the blade. When the text says “Down—steadily down it crept” (The Pit and the Pendulum, paragraph 31), it shows this directly. The repeated "Down—steadily down it crept" makes the reader endure each swing, so the escape feels earned even though the final rescue, "An outstretched arm caught my own," comes from outside.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the story to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

contentNotes.teacherNote: Sensitive content: Torture; rats. Preview the story, tell students in advance, and allow a pass on reading aloud. Keep discussion on how the writer uses these elements, not on graphic detail.
contentNotes.studentPreview: Heads-up: this story includes torture; rats.
contentNotes.suggestedLanguage: “Why does the writer include this, and what does it make us notice?”
